issues.description: The abstract, title, current-study section, discussion, and limitations all describe the sample as a 'national probability sample' or 'general population sample,' but the Methods section explicitly states participants were recruited 'through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington' with a mean age of 19.42 years and 68% female. These demographics are diagnostic of a university convenience sample, not a nationally representative one. The entire comparative framing of the paper—that it advances on Stanley et al. [14] because it uses a general-population rather than student sample—is therefore invalid. Conclusions about generalizability, and claims that the stronger SDO effect (relative to RWA) reflects what happens in the general population, are wholly unsupported.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington... the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.description: The reported sample size of N = 374 is mathematically incompatible with the confidence intervals presented in Table 1. For example, the reported 95% CI for the SDO mean is [2.58, 2.63] with SD = 0.96. A half-width of 0.025 implies √N ≈ 1.96 × 0.96 / 0.025 = 75.3, i.e., N ≈ 5,670. Analogous calculations from the RWA mean CI and the SDO–RWA correlation CI converge on an actual sample of approximately 5,700–6,200. The note that confidence intervals are 'based on 1000 iterations' (bootstrap) and the reference to the NZAVS website suggest the data originate from the NZAVS national panel (thousands of participants), but the reported N = 374 has been inserted—likely from a different study. The stated N, and any statistical conclusions that depend on it (e.g., the power justification for p < .05), are unreliable.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study... Mean [SDO] 2.60 [2.58, 2.63]... Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations.

issues.description: The title, abstract, and current-study section refer to 'a five-year' study, yet the methods describe 'five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).' Five university semesters span only 2.5 years, not five. Moreover, 2009–2013 represents five annual measurement occasions separated by four years. None of these is accurately described as 'five years.' This inconsistency makes the measurement intervals ambiguous and undermines the claim that the study captures long-term temporal effects.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: The abstract, study title, and current-study section describe the outcome as 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment,' and throughout the results the variable is called WILL ('willingness to make sacrifices for the environment'). However, the Measures section describes a scale of environmental *concern*—'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?' Concern and behavioural willingness/sacrifice are distinct constructs with different predictors and correlates. The mislabelling means readers cannot evaluate what was actually measured, and the theoretical interpretation (e.g., 'the motivation to exploit the environment') may not follow from the actual data.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'

issues.description: Throughout the discussion and conclusion, the authors make strong causal claims ('there is a causal pathway,' 'SDO having a causal effect,' 'the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future'). Cross-lagged panel models cannot establish causation. Critically, the standard CLPM as used here conflates within-person dynamics with stable between-person differences: if two variables share a correlated stable trait component, the cross-lagged paths will appear significant even in the complete absence of within-person causal influence (Hamaker, Kuiper, & Grasman, 2015). The Random Intercept CLPM, which would separate these components, is not considered. The causal language is therefore not warranted.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism... with our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes.

issues.description: The central claim of the paper—that SDO is a *significantly stronger* predictor than RWA—is directly contradicted by the authors' own model-comparison test. The chi-square difference test constraining both paths to equality produced χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126, a non-significant result. Despite this, the authors write 'we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor.' In the conclusion, this has escalated to 'SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA.' The statistical test does not support significance; the authors' interpretation is inconsistent with their own analysis.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The CFI of .86 is below the conventionally required minimum of .90 (often .95 for acceptable/good fit). The authors dismiss this by attributing it to 'model complexity,' but CFI is explicitly designed to penalise for complexity; a CFI of .86 indicates that the model fits substantially worse than a saturated model, which is a meaningful misfit indicator. Accepting the model on the basis of RMSEA alone while acknowledging poor CFI is not standard practice and should be explicitly justified with additional sensitivity analyses or an alternative model.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ²(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The reported 90% CI for RMSEA is [.025, .026], a half-width of only .0005. This is implausibly narrow for any SEM; RMSEA CIs are typically several hundredths wide. This appears to be a typographical or copy-paste error (e.g., the lower bound may have been misread from the output). An incorrect CI for RMSEA precludes assessment of whether the model meets close-fit criteria.

The chi-square for the SDO–RWA bidirectional comparison is reported as χ²(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001. A chi-square of over 15,000 on 1 degree of freedom is implausible for a model-comparison test in behavioural research and almost certainly reflects either a software error, a misread of Mplus output (e.g., confusing a scaling correction factor or a log-likelihood with a chi-square), or a typographical error. Reporting this value without comment or verification seriously undermines the credibility of the analysis.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (χ²(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.description: In a five-wave longitudinal structural model, measurement invariance across time is a prerequisite for meaningful comparison of latent means and interpretation of cross-lagged paths. If the factor loadings or intercepts of SDO, RWA, or environmentalism items shift over time, observed changes in cross-lagged paths confound genuine attitude change with changes in how constructs are measured. No test of configural, metric, or scalar invariance is reported, and no reference is made to this requirement.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The authors state that listwise deletion was used for missing data. In a longitudinal study with five waves, listwise deletion typically discards a substantial proportion of participants and—unless data are missing completely at random (MCAR), a strong and rarely met assumption—produces biased estimates. Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) is the recommended approach for CLPM in Mplus and makes only the weaker MAR assumption. No attrition analysis is reported, no justification for MCAR is provided, and the sample size at each wave is not reported. The combination of attrition and listwise deletion could seriously bias the estimates.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: One RWA item was not administered at Time 2 but was included at all other time points. Using a six-item scale at Times 1, 3, 4, and 5 but a five-item scale at Time 2 means the RWA composite score at T2 is not directly comparable to the others. This violates the assumption of parallel measurement across time points central to the cross-lagged model and could produce artefactual changes in the RWA autoregressive and cross-lagged paths around T2. The authors do not address how they handled this inconsistency (e.g., mean imputation, prorating, or item parcelling).
issues.quote: The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: observed-variable path analysis ignores measurement error
issues.description: The model uses composite scale scores as single observed indicators in a path model rather than specifying latent variables with multiple indicators. This approach treats the composites as perfectly reliable, which they are not (e.g., SDO α = .69, RWA α = .70). Measurement error in observed variables attenuates regression coefficients and inflates standard errors in an unsystematic way, biasing cross-lagged estimates. Latent variable SEM would estimate and correct for measurement error, producing more accurate structural parameters.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: The Methods section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings,' but the caption for Figure 1 reads 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These two thresholds are contradictory. It is unclear which was actually used to determine significance, and the discrepancy could affect which paths are claimed to be significant.
issues.quote: We adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings. ... All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: In the Results section, the precision of the regression coefficients is reported using 'SD' (e.g., 'B = -.11, SD = .01'). In the context of a regression or SEM output, this quantity is the standard error of the estimate (SE), not the standard deviation of a distribution. The term SD is incorrect and misleading, because standard errors and standard deviations have different interpretations and different uses in inference.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: The Methods section states 'We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances,' but Figure 1's caption is titled 'Unstandardized parameters.' These cannot simultaneously be true. It is unclear which parameters are actually displayed. The distinction matters: unstandardised and standardised coefficients have different interpretations, and comparing the magnitudes of SDO and RWA paths requires careful attention to their scaling.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances. ... Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).

issues.description: The assumption of stationarity (time-invariant cross-lagged and autoregressive parameters) is imposed on the model without being tested. Whether this constraint is supported by the data should be evaluated by comparing the constrained model to an unconstrained model. Given the five-year span and the possibility that the SDO–environmentalism relationship strengthens or weakens over time (or that societal events between 2009 and 2013 differentially affect the relationships), this assumption requires empirical support.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.description: The sentence 'We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point' appears substantively twice in the Data Analysis section, the second time as 'Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.' This verbatim repetition suggests a copy-paste editing error and leaves ambiguity about whether additional constraints (beyond those already stated) were also applied.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: The environmentalism variable is described as comprising two items from Liu and Sibley's environmental concern scale. With only two items, Cronbach's alpha equals the correlation between the items rescaled by the Spearman-Brown formula; a reliability of .76 is plausible but the extremely limited item pool (n = 2) means the construct is weakly sampled and the measure lacks content validity for a broad concept like 'environmentalism' or 'willingness to sacrifice.' The authors do not justify why only two items were used or whether these items adequately represent the construct.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'

issues.description: For a five-wave longitudinal study, attrition rate and the demographic or attitudinal profile of completers versus dropouts are essential for interpreting results. This information is entirely absent from the paper. Given that listwise deletion was used, results apply only to the subset completing all five waves. If attrition is related to the study variables (e.g., those lower in SDO are more likely to drop out), estimates of the cross-lagged effects will be biased.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.subcategory: bootstrap CI procedure undisclosed in methods
issues.description: The note on Table 1 states that confidence intervals are 'based on 1000 iterations,' indicating bootstrapped CIs. However, the Data Analysis section contains no mention of bootstrap resampling. The procedure for generating these CIs is not described: what was bootstrapped (the sample, the parameters?), which statistic, and whether the bootstrap CIs are percentile, bias-corrected, or accelerated. This omission prevents replication.
issues.quote: Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations.

issues.description: The internal consistency of the SDO scale (α = .69) is below the conventional minimum of .70. While the authors acknowledge this in a general way ('Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case'), they do not discuss the implications for the precision of the cross-lagged estimates or whether the items chosen constitute a validated short form of SDO6. The scale's reliability also affects the power to detect cross-lagged effects, as more measurement error attenuates true path coefficients.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures.

issues.description: All three constructs (SDO, RWA, environmentalism) are assessed via self-report Likert items in the same survey administration at each wave. Common method variance (CMV) inflates zero-order correlations between constructs measured in the same session and can also affect longitudinal estimates if the consistency motive operates within but not across waves. The authors do not acknowledge CMV as a potential confound or employ any procedural or statistical remedies.
issues.quote: As our research was survey-based, participants' responses were restricted to Likert-type responses to question items.

issues.subcategory: large-sample significance inflation not properly handled
issues.description: The authors state 'Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05.' With a very large N (implied by the CIs to be ~6,000), virtually all non-zero effects will reach p < .05. The RWA cross-lagged coefficient of B = -.02 is statistically significant but may be trivially small in practical terms. Effect sizes and practical significance should be the primary focus. The authors do not report standardised effect sizes for the cross-lagged paths, nor do they discuss the magnitude of the RWA effect in practical terms.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.description: The authors briefly raise the possibility that a third variable (e.g., perceived resource scarcity, economic recession) could explain the bidirectional ideology–environmentalism association but then defer this to future research. Given that the paper makes causal claims, alternative explanations should be engaged with more seriously. In particular, political events during 2009–2013 (the global financial crisis, prominent climate debates) could have differentially affected endorsers of SDO/RWA and environmentalism in ways the model cannot disentangle.
issues.quote: Specifically, it is possible that something related both to ideological and environmental attitudes could drive changes in each variable independently, hence explaining the apparent causal relations.

issues.description: The Strengths and Limitations section states 'Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.' This claim is false on two grounds: (1) the sample is an introductory psychology pool, not a nationally representative sample; and (2) even if it were NZAVS data, the NZAVS overrepresents educated, Pākehā, female, and middle-aged New Zealanders relative to the census. Claiming 'high generalisability' overstates what the data support.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The manuscript contains multiple typographical errors that affect readability and professionalism: 'stonger' (Results; should be 'stronger'), 'analagous' (Discussion; should be 'analogous'), 'sarcity' (Discussion; should be 'scarcity'), 'situatoinal' (Discussion; should be 'situational'), 'nonexistant' (Discussion; should be 'nonexistent'), and 'effect people's livelihoods' (Discussion; should be 'affect'). These errors suggest insufficient proofreading.
issues.quote: these analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships, and suggest that SDO has a stonger influence... resource sarcity and economic recession... These situatoinal factors... any relation between SDO and RWA is likely weak or nonexistant... effect people's livelihoods

issues.description: Reference [26] ('Sibley C. New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study.') contains no year, publisher, URL, DOI, or other locating information. Reference [29] (Mplus user's guide) is described as the 'Sixth edition' with a date range of '1998–2010,' yet the text specifies Mplus version 7.3, which was released after 2010 and corresponds to the seventh edition of the manual. These inconsistencies prevent readers from locating or verifying the cited sources.
issues.quote: Sibley C. New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study. ... Muthén LK, Muthén BO. Mplus user's guide. Sixth edition. Los Angeles, CA: Muthén & Muthén, 1998-2010.

issues.subcategory: cross-lagged panel model not adequately described
issues.description: The Methods section does not specify whether the autoregressive paths were also constrained to equality across time (i.e., whether the model is fully stationary or only partially constrained). It states that cross-lagged paths and residual variances are constrained, but omits mention of the autoregressive parameters. For a stationary CLPM, all parameters should be constrained, and the model description must be complete enough for independent replication. The partial description leaves the model unverifiable.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant. We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time.
